blocks.text: Support Vector Regression introduced a genuinely different algorithm family, but still fundamentally fit a continuous function shaped by kernels and margins. Decision tree regression breaks from every technique covered so far in this module in a genuinely more fundamental way, producing no equation or coefficients at all, instead splitting the feature space into regions through a genuine sequence of simple, yes or no threshold questions.

This topic covers exactly how a decision tree genuinely splits data into regions, how it turns those regions into an actual prediction, variance reduction, the specific rule genuinely used to choose each split, directly echoing the impurity reduction concept first covered back in Tree-Based Selection, a genuinely refreshing real advantage, no feature scaling required at all, and a real, honest weakness, this technique real tendency to overfit when grown too deep.
1. How a Decision Tree Actually Splits Data

blocks.alt: All data splits on a feature into region 1 and region 2

blocks.text: Starting with all genuine training data together, a decision tree genuinely asks a simple, yes or no threshold question about one feature, is square footage above 1500, for instance, splitting the data into two genuine resulting groups based on the answer. This genuine process then repeats within each resulting group, asking further questions, building a tree of splits that progressively divides the entire feature space into smaller, more specific regions.

This is genuinely, fundamentally different from every earlier regression topic, there is no continuous function being fit at all, only a genuine sequence of simple, direct comparisons that carve up the data into distinct regions.
2. Turning a Region Into an Actual Prediction

blocks.alt: A final region becomes its average target value

blocks.text: Once every split has genuinely been made, each final region, called a leaf, contains a genuine subset of the original training points that all landed there through the exact same sequence of yes or no answers. A prediction for any new point genuinely follows that same sequence of questions down to its matching leaf, and the prediction returned is genuinely the average target value of whichever training points originally landed in that exact same leaf.

This is genuinely a completely different notion of prediction from every earlier topic, there is no formula being evaluated, only a genuine lookup of which region a new point falls into, followed by a genuine average of that region historical training values.
3. Choosing Each Split: Variance Reduction

blocks.alt: A candidate split is evaluated by variance reduction to choose the best split

blocks.text: At every genuine split point, a decision tree regressor considers candidate questions and picks whichever one genuinely reduces the variance of the target values within the resulting child regions the most, producing genuinely tighter, more internally consistent groups. This is directly, genuinely the same core idea as the impurity reduction covered back in Tree-Based Selection, just measuring variance for a continuous target instead of a classification impurity measure like Gini or entropy.

This connection is worth holding onto directly, the exact same recursive, greedy splitting mechanism that produced feature importance scores in that earlier topic is genuinely the same mechanism building the actual predictive tree structure here.

blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example

blocks.alt: House data splits on size to produce a price prediction

blocks.text: Fitting scikit-learn DecisionTreeRegressor directly, with genuinely no scaling applied at all, shows this technique in practice.

code.content:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
import pandas as pd

X = pd.DataFrame({"square_feet": [900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400]})
y = pd.Series([250000, 310000, 360000, 410000, 460000, 510000])

model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2)
model.fit(X, y)

print("Predicted price for 1650 sqft:", model.predict([[1650]])[0])

blocks.text: No scaling was genuinely applied anywhere in this example, and none was genuinely needed, the tree simply compares raw square footage values against a learned threshold directly, with no distance calculation or coefficient magnitude involved at all.

blocks.text: 5. A Genuinely Refreshing Advantage: No Scaling Required

blocks.alt: A decision tree requires no feature scaling

blocks.text: Every feature comparison inside a decision tree genuinely happens one feature at a time, is this single value above or below a threshold, never combining multiple features into a genuine distance calculation the way support vector regression, PCA, or LDA all genuinely require. This means feature scale becomes genuinely, completely irrelevant to how a tree actually makes its splitting decisions.

This is a genuinely real, refreshing practical advantage after several consecutive topics in this module that specifically required feature scaling, decision trees, and the ensemble techniques built on top of them covered next, genuinely skip that entire preprocessing requirement altogether.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Decision trees, and the ensemble methods built on them covered later in this course, genuinely never require feature scaling. This is a real, practical exception to a rule that has applied to nearly every other technique in this module.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuine, Natural Advantage: Nonlinearity and Interactions for Free

blocks.alt: A decision tree captures nonlinearity for free

blocks.text: Because a tree genuinely builds its regions through a sequence of splits, it naturally captures nonlinear relationships directly, with no manual polynomial feature expansion required, exactly the manual work Polynomial Regression needed. It genuinely captures feature interactions naturally too, since later splits can genuinely depend on the outcome of earlier ones, with no manual interaction feature required either, exactly the manual work Interaction Features covered.

This is a genuinely real, structural advantage worth appreciating directly, a decision tree gets both of these real capabilities essentially for free, as a natural consequence of how it is built, rather than requiring the deliberate feature engineering work earlier topics in this course needed to achieve something similar.
7. The Real Weakness: Overfitting When Grown Too Deep

blocks.alt: A tree grown too deep overfits the training data

blocks.text: A genuinely shallow tree, with few splits, produces broad, sensible regions that genuinely generalize reasonably well to new data. A genuinely deep tree, with many splits, can end up creating tiny, highly specific regions that genuinely memorize individual training points rather than capturing any real, general pattern, exactly the same overfitting concept covered throughout this course, now showing up as excessive tree depth rather than excessive polynomial degree.

This real weakness is genuinely controlled directly through hyperparameters like max_depth, limiting how many splits deep the tree can grow, and min_samples_leaf, requiring a genuine minimum number of training points in every final region, both covered in far more practical depth in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always set a genuine max_depth or min_samples_leaf when fitting a decision tree regressor for a real project. An unconstrained tree genuinely grows until it perfectly memorizes the training data.

blocks.text: 8. Decision Tree Regression Versus What Comes Next

This topic introduced a genuinely fundamental departure from every earlier regression technique, rule based regions instead of any continuous equation, with real, natural advantages around nonlinearity, interactions, and scaling, alongside a real, honest overfitting weakness tied directly to tree depth.

The next topic, Random Forest Regression, addresses that exact real weakness directly, building genuinely many trees together and averaging their predictions, extending this topic core idea into a considerably more stable, reliable ensemble.

items: Decision tree regression genuinely splits the feature space into regions through a sequence of threshold questions.
A prediction is genuinely the average target value of training points in the matching final leaf region.
Splits are genuinely chosen by variance reduction, directly echoing impurity reduction from Tree-Based Selection.
Decision trees genuinely require no feature scaling at all, unlike most techniques covered earlier in this module.
They genuinely capture nonlinearity and feature interactions naturally, without manual feature engineering.
The next topic, Random Forest Regression, genuinely builds an ensemble of trees to fix this real overfitting weakness.
